# Dividing one duration by another, compiled and run as Go, then run again on
# the interpreter.
#
# testdata/unit_duration_ratio.txtar says what each target generates; this says
# the answers agree, and it is the claim that matters because the four runners
# carry a duration differently -- an integer time.Duration on Go, a Long on
# Kotlin, a number on JavaScript, a magnitude per base in the interpreter.
#
# Go and Kotlin emitted the host's integer division into a float, which does
# not compile; the interpreter refused the operation outright with "cannot
# divide by a unit value", so `--platform=none` reported an error rather than a
# wrong number. Both are why a golden alone is not enough here.
#
# `fraction` is the one that separates widening before the divide from
# converting after it: 250ms over 1500ms is a sixth, and an integer division
# reports zero.

sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

-- app.sngl --
import . "sngl:test"
import ui "sngl:ui"
import time "sngl:time"

component main ui.node {
    var span time.duration = 1500ms
    var period time.duration = 250ms
    var ratio = 0.0
    var fraction = 0.0
    var halved = 0

    effect(@mount {
        ratio = span / period
        fraction = period / span
        halved = int(span / 2)
    })

    ui.text(value="{ratio}")
}

// unit / unit is the dimensionless ratio of the two magnitudes.
func testTheRatioOfTwoDurationsIsAFloat(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.ratio == 6.0)
}

// And a float rather than a truncating divide, which is the half no target got
// right by accident.
func testARatioBelowOneIsNotTruncated(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.fraction > 0.16 && c.fraction < 0.17)
}

// unit / number is still that unit, the other half of the rule.
func testADurationOverANumberIsADuration(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.halved == 750)
}

ui.window {
    main
}
-- testrun/bubbletea/go/app.sngl/main/1 --
